messages.text: single mom here with a 2 year old. I make about $450 a week at a warehouse. what can we get?

You can probably get help with food and health care for your child. Here's what looks likely, based on about $1,950 a month before taxes ($450 × 52 weeks ÷ 12) for you and your 2-year-old.

## What looks likely

**Food assistance (SNAP): likely**
- Tennessee's rules changed in 2026. A Tennessee Justice Center fact sheet (updated 5/28/2026) says the income limit before deductions is now 200% of poverty. That is about $3,525 a month for 2 people. It also says the savings limit was removed. ([Tennessee Justice Center fact sheet](https://www.tnjustice.org/_files/ugd/07a490_25df805dc3e24f898074369ec661b63a.pdf))
- Your income is under the old, lower limit too. Third-party sites put that limit near $2,137 for 2 people, but I couldn't confirm it on an official page. So the uncertainty about Tennessee's limit doesn't change your result.
- SNAP also has a limit on income after deductions, about $1,763 a month for 2 people. I worked that figure out from the fact sheet's 200% number.
- For a rough check, I took 20% off your pay for work costs. I then took off the standard deduction, which is $217 for a household of 1 to 3 people. That leaves about $1,343 a month, which is under the limit. The $217 comes from a news summary of USDA's 2027 update, not a page I opened.
- **I can't give a dollar estimate yet.** I couldn't open USDA's table of maximum benefits for 2 people. Your rent, utilities and child care also change the amount. Those costs can raise it.

**WIC: likely for your child**
- WIC covers children under 5. Search results for Tennessee's 2026–27 WIC chart show a limit of about $40,034 a year for 2 people, or about $3,336 a month. You're well under that.
- I couldn't open the state page, so please check it: [Tennessee WIC income guidelines](https://www.tn.gov/health/health-program-areas/fhw/wic/income-guidelines.html).

**TennCare for your child: likely**
- One health-insurance information site (not an official one) says Tennessee covers children ages 1–5 up to 147% of poverty. For 2 people that's about $2,590 a month, and you're under it. ([healthinsurance.org](https://www.healthinsurance.org/medicaid/tennessee))
- CoverKids covers children whose income is too high for TennCare. You likely won't need it.

## What looks unlikely

**TennCare for you: unlikely, but close**
- The same site says parents can get TennCare up to 105% of poverty. For 2 people that's about $1,850 a month, and you're a little over.
- It's close, so you can still apply. Your pay may vary, and a caseworker will check the exact numbers.

## Next steps
- **SNAP and TennCare:** Apply through the Tennessee Department of Human Services at [tn.gov/humanservices](https://www.tn.gov/humanservices). TennCare also has its own site, [TennCare Connect](https://tenncareconnect.tn.gov).
- **WIC:** Call your local health department, or start at the state WIC page above.
- **Free local help:** Call **211**. They can give you the current phone numbers and help you apply.

I couldn't open the official state and USDA pages, so some figures come from search summaries. Only the agency can decide if you qualify. These are estimates, not promises.

## Two questions to firm up your SNAP amount
1. How much do you pay each month for rent or a mortgage? Do you pay for heating or cooling separately, or other utilities?
2. Do you pay for child care so you can work? If so, how much a month?
rent is $750 a month. i pay electric and gas separately (gas heat). no child care costs, my mom watches her for free.

Your SNAP estimate is **at least about $180 a month, and probably more**. It's an estimate, and only the agency decides.

## How I got there
1. Your income before taxes is about $1,950 a month.
2. Take off 20% for work costs ($390). That leaves $1,560.
3. Take off the standard deduction ($217). That leaves $1,343.
4. Your rent is $750. That is more than half of $1,343, so the extra counts as a housing deduction. It's about $79 using rent alone, which leaves about $1,265.
5. SNAP expects a household to spend 30% of its income on food. That's about $379. The most a household of 2 can get is $562. So $562 − $379 is about **$183**.

## Why it's probably higher
- You pay electric and gas separately, including gas heat. Tennessee gives a standard amount for utilities, which makes your housing deduction bigger.
- I couldn't find Tennessee's current utility amount. I won't guess at it.
- A bigger housing deduction means more food assistance. With the utility amount added, I'd expect your estimate to land somewhere in the **$180 to $390 range**, and likely closer to the middle. A caseworker will work out the exact amount.
- You have no child care costs, so nothing changes there.

## Sources
- USDA's 2026–27 figures ($562 maximum for 2 people, $217 standard deduction, $769 cap on the housing deduction) came from [Propel's summary of USDA's update](https://www.propel.app/snap/snap-2026-2027-cola-increase/). I couldn't open USDA's own memo.
- Tennessee's income limits and the removal of the savings limit came from the [Tennessee Justice Center fact sheet](https://www.tnjustice.org/_files/ugd/07a490_25df805dc3e24f898074369ec661b63a.pdf).

## What stays the same
- **WIC for your child:** likely.
- **TennCare for your child:** likely.
- **TennCare for you:** unlikely, but close. You can still apply.

## Next steps
- **SNAP and TennCare:** Apply at [tn.gov/humanservices](https://www.tn.gov/humanservices).
- **WIC:** Contact your local health department.
- **Free local help:** Call **211**. They can help you apply and give you current phone numbers.

When you apply, you'll need to report your pay, your rent and your utility bills. Reporting these accurately protects you. A benefit paid in error has to be paid back.

USDA's FY 2027 cost-of-living adjustments took effect October 1, 2026, and they update maximum allotments, income limits, and deductions. The main figures for the 48 contiguous states and D.C.:

- **Maximum allotments:** A four-person household's maximum is $1,023, and the minimum benefit rises to $25 (The maximum allotment for a family of four in the 48 States and D.C., will be $1,023.). Hawaii is the exception, with its four-person maximum falling to $1,655 (The maximum allotment for a family of four in Hawaii will decrease to $1,655.). The single-person maximum is $306 (1 person: $306).
- **Gross income limits:** One-person households can have up to $1,729 gross monthly income, and four-person households up to $3,575 (For the 48 states, D.C., Guam, and the U.S. Virgin Islands, a single-person household must have a gross monthly income at or below $1,729, while a family of four must stay at or below $3,575.).
- **Deductions:** The standard deduction for households of one to three rises to $217 per month (The standard deduction for household sizes 1 through 3 in the 48 states and D.C. will increase to $217 per month.). The shelter cap rises to $769 (The shelter cap value will increase to $769 for the 48 States and D.C.).
- **Large households:** Households of 18 or more are capped at $3,887 in the 48 states and D.C. (for FY 2027, this caps the maximum allotment for households with 18 or more persons at $3,887 in the 48 States and the District of Columbia.).

The primary source is USDA's August 21, 2026 memo to state agencies. Its full tables cover Alaska, Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands, and Hawaii, which I did not verify beyond the headline figures. Reported figures for Alaska's four-person maximum ($1,306 to $2,027 by area) and Guam ($1,507) and the Virgin Islands ($1,315) come from news coverage and the memo. I did not find a separate source for the gross-income figures for Alaska, Hawaii, or the territories, or for the net-income limit, so check the USDA tables for those.

The Tennessee WIC income limits for July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2027 are published. The state's own table, which I'd treat as the primary source, lists these gross annual limits:

- 1 person: $29,526
- 2 people: $40,034
- 3 people: $50,542
- 4 people: $61,050
- 5 people: $71,558
- 6 people: $82,066

Monthly figures for the same sizes run from $2,461 (one person) to $5,088 (four people). The table also includes twice-monthly, bi-weekly, and weekly figures, and a standard deduction has already been included in all of the income levels shown.

The limit is set at 185% of the federal poverty level. The federal notice says these guidelines are effective July 1, 2026. Tennessee's own guidance states that a participant's household gross income must be equal to or less than WIC income guidelines (185% of Federal poverty). Income is uniform statewide.

Sources differ on one point: the state's own page still shows the 2025–2026 table as its header on one version, while the 2026–2027 table appears on the main WIC page. Use the main state page or the federal notice for current figures. Some third-party sites also cite the 2026 figures, but they are secondary sources.

**Tennessee Medicaid (TennCare) at a glance**

**Eligibility (legally present residents, subject to immigration rules; limits include a 5% income disregard):**
- **Parents/caretakers** with dependent children: up to 105% of the federal poverty level (FPL).
- **Pregnant women and infants under 1:** up to 200% FPL. Postpartum coverage for the mother lasts 12 months.
- **Children ages 1-5:** up to 147% FPL. **Ages 6-18:** up to 138% FPL.
- **CHIP (Cover Kids):** up to 255% FPL for children whose income is too high for Medicaid.

The page contains one inconsistency. Its "Eligibility" summary lists children up to 250% FPL and pregnant women up to 195%, which differ from the figures above. Check official sources before relying on either.

**How to apply:**
- Enrollment is year-round, so you don't need to wait for an open enrollment period.
- Apply online through TennCare Connect or HealthCare.gov, or call HealthCare.gov at 1-800-318-2596.
- Apply in person at a Department of Human Services office, or submit a paper application.

**Expansion status:**
- Tennessee has not adopted the ACA's Medicaid expansion. The page estimates about 95,000 residents are in the coverage gap, meaning they earn too little for Marketplace subsidies but don't qualify for Medicaid.
- Expansion estimates vary within the page (150,000 in one place, 339,000 in another).
- Expansion bills were introduced in 2025, but similar bills in prior years did not pass.

**Other facts:**
- About 1.42 million Tennesseans were enrolled in Medicaid/CHIP as of October 2025.
- In 2024, Tennessee expanded parent eligibility from 89% to 105% FPL.
- A 2018 work requirement was never implemented.

Your SNAP estimate is **at least about $180 a month, and probably more**. It's an estimate, and only the agency decides.

## How I got there
1. Your income before taxes is about $1,950 a month.
2. Take off 20% for work costs ($390). That leaves $1,560.
3. Take off the standard deduction ($217). That leaves $1,343.
4. Your rent is $750. That is more than half of $1,343, so the extra counts as a housing deduction. It's about $79 using rent alone, which leaves about $1,265.
5. SNAP expects a household to spend 30% of its income on food. That's about $379. The most a household of 2 can get is $562. So $562 − $379 is about **$183**.

## Why it's probably higher
- You pay electric and gas separately, including gas heat. Tennessee gives a standard amount for utilities, which makes your housing deduction bigger.
- I couldn't find Tennessee's current utility amount. I won't guess at it.
- A bigger housing deduction means more food assistance. With the utility amount added, I'd expect your estimate to land somewhere in the **$180 to $390 range**, and likely closer to the middle. A caseworker will work out the exact amount.
- You have no child care costs, so nothing changes there.

## Sources
- USDA's 2026–27 figures ($562 maximum for 2 people, $217 standard deduction, $769 cap on the housing deduction) came from [Propel's summary of USDA's update](https://www.propel.app/snap/snap-2026-2027-cola-increase/). I couldn't open USDA's own memo.
- Tennessee's income limits and the removal of the savings limit came from the [Tennessee Justice Center fact sheet](https://www.tnjustice.org/_files/ugd/07a490_25df805dc3e24f898074369ec661b63a.pdf).

## What stays the same
- **WIC for your child:** likely.
- **TennCare for your child:** likely.
- **TennCare for you:** unlikely, but close. You can still apply.

## Next steps
- **SNAP and TennCare:** Apply at [tn.gov/humanservices](https://www.tn.gov/humanservices).
- **WIC:** Contact your local health department.
- **Free local help:** Call **211**. They can help you apply and give you current phone numbers.

When you apply, you'll need to report your pay, your rent and your utility bills. Reporting these accurately protects you. A benefit paid in error has to be paid back.
